message.content: {"summary":"A strong submission overall. Q2 was excellent with scenario-specific trade-offs, and Q1, Q3, Q4, Q5 and Q6 all showed sound method. To lift marks: make the availability response measure measurable, include the non-payment components in Q3(c), apply CAP correctly in Q5, add a negative consequence to the ADR, and keep every answer within 150 words.","next_steps":["In Q3(c), multiply the payment-pair availability (0.999975) by the other three components (0.9995×0.999×0.9995) to get the end-to-end availability (~99.80%, ~1.5 h downtime) rather than reporting the payment pair alone.","In Q5, reframe the CAP argument: partition tolerance cannot be given up; during a partition you must choose between consistency and availability, so justify each choice as C or A under partition.","In Q6, add at least one negative consequence (e.g. delayed outlet notification, duplicate-order handling, extra infrastructure) to balance the ADR.","Trim Q2 and Q4 to 150 words each, stating any assumptions explicitly, and make the Q1 availability response measure measurable (e.g. '99.5% uptime measured monthly')."],"criteria":{"C1":"You chose suitable attributes (performance and availability) with good scenario-based justification, and your performance scenario was fully six-part and measurable. To reach Excellent, both response measures must be measurable: 'stay up most of the time' is not. Replace it with a quantified target, e.g. '99.5% availability measured monthly', and keep the six-part structure for both scenarios.","C2":"Excellent work. Your modular monolith recommendation was clearly justified with two trade-offs tied to the scenario — the five-developer team size and the root causes of the known problems — and you acknowledged the downside (no independent scaling, one bug can crash the process). This meets the Excellent standard; just watch the 150-word limit (see C7).","C3":"Parts (a) and (b) were correct with working shown (99.30%, 5.0 h). Part (c) reported only the payment-pair availability (99.9975%) and dropped the other three components. The end-to-end availability is 0.9980010×0.999975 ≈ 99.80%, about 1.5 h downtime per month. Your method is sound — show the full product in part (c) to reach Excellent.","C4":"You named the circuit breaker correctly, explained its states and thresholds well, and applied it convincingly to the outage with a realistic user-facing message. The missing element for full marks is an explicit drawback or tuning consideration — e.g. false trips on slow (rather than failed) calls, or how to choose the failure threshold and timeout values.","C5":"Both choices were reasonable and you named concrete techniques (Redis TTL cache; idempotency keys), which is good. However, CAP was misapplied: 'giving up partition tolerance' is not an option — partitions will happen, so the real choice during a partition is between consistency and availability. Restate each choice as C-over-A or A-over-C under partition to reach Excellent.","C6":"Your ADR had all three sections, scenario-specific context and a clear decision, and the positive consequence (faster order placement) was well stated. What held it at Proficient was the one-sided consequences: add at least one negative consequence, such as eventual outlet notification, duplicate-order handling, or extra infrastructure cost.","C7":"Your headings, ordering and IEEE citations were correct, but Q2 (~200 words) and Q4 (~160 words) exceeded the 150-word limit and no assumptions were stated. Practise writing tight, prioritised answers: state assumptions in one line, cut generic textbook material, and count words before submitting to reach the Excellent level."}}
